claim: RhopH2 is a membrane-associated protein that can be partially extracted by Na2CO3 at pH 11
source: Each member of the RhopH complex is membrane-associated but can be partially extracted by Na2CO3 at pH 11 (Figure 1A), suggesting distinct pools are peripheral and integral to membranes.
evidence: Supported by biochemical extraction data shown in Figure 1A and described in the text

claim: RhopH3 is a membrane-associated protein that can be partially extracted by Na2CO3 at pH 11
source: Each member of the RhopH complex is membrane-associated but can be partially extracted by Na2CO3 at pH 11 (Figure 1A), suggesting distinct pools are peripheral and integral to membranes.
evidence: Supported by biochemical extraction data shown in Figure 1A and described in the text

claim: CLAG3 is a membrane-associated protein that can be partially extracted by Na2CO3 at pH 11
source: Each member of the RhopH complex is membrane-associated but can be partially extracted by Na2CO3 at pH 11 (Figure 1A), suggesting distinct pools are peripheral and integral to membranes.
evidence: Supported by biochemical extraction data shown in Figure 1A and described in the text

claim: RhopH2 and RhopH3 exist as distinct pools that are peripheral and integral to membranes
source: Each member of the RhopH complex is membrane-associated but can be partially extracted by Na2CO3 at pH 11 (Figure 1A), suggesting distinct pools are peripheral and integral to membranes.
evidence: Inferred from differential extraction behavior with Na2CO3

claim: CLAG3 is cleaved by pronase E treatment at a variant surface-exposed loop
source: While pronase E treatment of infected cells confirmed CLAG3 proteolysis at a variant surface-exposed loop (Figure 1A; Nguitragool et al., 2014), RhopH2 and RhopH3 were not cleaved, suggesting that they are not exposed at the host membrane.
evidence: Supported by protease susceptibility data in Figure 1A and cited reference

claim: RhopH2 is not cleaved by pronase E treatment
source: While pronase E treatment of infected cells confirmed CLAG3 proteolysis at a variant surface-exposed loop (Figure 1A; Nguitragool et al., 2014), RhopH2 and RhopH3 were not cleaved, suggesting that they are not exposed at the host membrane.
evidence: Supported by protease susceptibility data in Figure 1A

claim: RhopH3 is not cleaved by pronase E treatment
source: While pronase E treatment of infected cells confirmed CLAG3 proteolysis at a variant surface-exposed loop (Figure 1A; Nguitragool et al., 2014), RhopH2 and RhopH3 were not cleaved, suggesting that they are not exposed at the host membrane.
evidence: Supported by protease susceptibility data in Figure 1A

claim: RhopH2 and RhopH3 are not exposed at the host membrane
source: While pronase E treatment of infected cells confirmed CLAG3 proteolysis at a variant surface-exposed loop (Figure 1A; Nguitragool et al., 2014), RhopH2 and RhopH3 were not cleaved, suggesting that they are not exposed at the host membrane.
evidence: Inferred from resistance to pronase E cleavage

claim: The resistance of RhopH2 and RhopH3 to pronase E is consistent with polymorphism at surface-exposed epitopes
source: The resistance of RhopH2 and RhopH3 to pronase E, the relative absence of polymorphisms in the genes that encode these proteins in P. falciparum clones (Iriko et al., 2008), and CLAG3 proteolysis at a variant motif are all consistent with polymorphism at surface-exposed epitopes; such polymorphisms are presumably selected by host immune attack.
evidence: Supported by protease data, genetic polymorphism data from cited reference, and inference about immune selection

claim: RhopH2, RhopH3, and CLAG3 localize to rhoptry organelles in daughter merozoites
source: Immunofluorescence microscopy confirmed packaging into rhoptries within schizont-infected cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging data in Figure 1B showing punctate labeling

claim: RhopH2, RhopH3, and CLAG3 traffic to the host membrane in maturing trophozoite-stage parasites
source: Imaging of maturing trophozoite-stage parasites also showed that these proteins traffic to the host membrane (Figure 1C), consistent with earlier localization studies (Vincensini et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging data in Figure 1C and cited reference

claim: Each RhopH gene is transcribed and translated only within schizonts
source: Because each gene is transcribed and translated only within schizonts, the protein found in these maturing trophozoites reflects transfer from the merozoite during invasion (Lustigman et al., 1988; Ling et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by cited references on gene expression timing

claim: RhopH proteins found in maturing trophozoites reflect transfer from the merozoite during invasion
source: Because each gene is transcribed and translated only within schizonts, the protein found in these maturing trophozoites reflects transfer from the merozoite during invasion (Lustigman et al., 1988; Ling et al., 2004).
evidence: Inferred from stage-specific gene expression and protein localization data

claim: About half of each RhopH protein is lost to the culture supernatant after invasion
source: To quantify this transfer, we performed stage-specific immunoblotting and found that about half of each protein was lost to the culture supernatant, where it associated with the ultracentrifugation pellet ('spent', Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative immunoblotting data in Figure 1D

claim: RhopH proteins lost to culture supernatant associate with the ultracentrifugation pellet
source: To quantify this transfer, we performed stage-specific immunoblotting and found that about half of each protein was lost to the culture supernatant, where it associated with the ultracentrifugation pellet ('spent', Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by fractionation and immunoblotting data in Figure 1D

claim: Each RhopH protein's abundance remains relatively constant throughout parasite maturation from ring to trophozoite stages
source: After invasion, each protein's abundance remained relatively constant throughout parasite maturation from ring to trophozoite stages (Figure 1D), consistent with biochemically stable proteins that do not undergo further synthesis until the schizont stage.
evidence: Supported by stage-specific immunoblotting data in Figure 1D

claim: RhopH proteins are biochemically stable and do not undergo further synthesis until the schizont stage
source: After invasion, each protein's abundance remained relatively constant throughout parasite maturation from ring to trophozoite stages (Figure 1D), consistent with biochemically stable proteins that do not undergo further synthesis until the schizont stage.
evidence: Inferred from constant protein abundance across developmental stages

claim: Neither rhoph2 nor rhoph3 genes could be disrupted by CRISPR-Cas9 transfection
source: Neither gene could be disrupted ('KO', Figure 1F) by transfection with two separate single guide RNAs (sgRNAs) designed from each gene's 5' end (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by PCR data in Figure 1F showing retention of wild-type sequence

claim: sgRNAs targeting rhoph2 and rhoph3 yielded robust integration of codon-optimized gene fragments that preserve the encoded protein sequences
source: At the same time, these sgRNAs yielded robust integration of a codon-optimized gene fragment that preserves the encoded protein sequences ('con'), indicating effective targeting of these genomic sites and tolerance for synonymous DNA changes.
evidence: Supported by PCR data in Figure 1F showing integration

claim: Both RhopH2 and RhopH3 serve essential functions
source: These findings suggest that both RhopH2 and RhopH3 serve essential functions.
evidence: Inferred from inability to generate knockouts despite effective sgRNA targeting

claim: R2glmS and R3glmS parasites carry the glmS riboswitch without residual wild-type sequence
source: We introduced glmS into each gene's 3' UTR using specific sgRNAs (Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1); limiting dilution clones, R2glmS and R3glmS, carried the riboswitch without residual wild-type sequence.
evidence: Supported by genetic integration data and clonal selection

claim: R2glmS and R3glmS parasites exhibit unchanged growth in the absence of GlcN
source: Both parasites exhibited unchanged growth in the absence of GlcN (data not shown), consistent with a benign distal modification of each gene.
evidence: Supported by growth assay data (not shown)

claim: GlcN treatment reduces RhopH2 to essentially undetectable levels in R2glmS schizont-infected cells
source: Immunoblotting revealed that this treatment reduced each targeted protein to essentially undetectable levels in schizont-infected cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2C

claim: GlcN treatment reduces RhopH3 to essentially undetectable levels in R3glmS schizont-infected cells
source: Immunoblotting revealed that this treatment reduced each targeted protein to essentially undetectable levels in schizont-infected cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2C

claim: GlcN treatment has no effect on RAP1 protein levels
source: This suppressor had no effect on RAP1, an unrelated membrane-associated rhoptry protein (Baldi et al., 2000), or on these proteins in untransfected parasites, indicating specific action at the introduced glmS riboswitch.
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2C and cited reference

claim: GlcN treatment of R2glmS abolishes CLAG3 protein
source: Remarkably, GlcN treatment of either R2glmS or R3glmS abolished not only the targeted gene product but also CLAG3, a third better-characterized member of the RhopH complex.
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2C

claim: GlcN treatment of R3glmS abolishes CLAG3 protein
source: Remarkably, GlcN treatment of either R2glmS or R3glmS abolished not only the targeted gene product but also CLAG3, a third better-characterized member of the RhopH complex.
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 2C

claim: RhopH2 has a more diffuse distribution and does not fully colocalize with RAP1 in GlcN-treated R3glmS parasites
source: While RhopH2 was still detected in the R3glmS knockdown, it did not fully colocalize with RAP1 but instead had a more diffuse distribution; this suggests that RhopH2 may be retained in the parasite endoplasmic reticulum if it fails to interact with RhopH3.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging data in Figure 2D

claim: RhopH2 may be retained in the parasite endoplasmic reticulum if it fails to interact with RhopH3
source: While RhopH2 was still detected in the R3glmS knockdown, it did not fully colocalize with RAP1 but instead had a more diffuse distribution; this suggests that RhopH2 may be retained in the parasite endoplasmic reticulum if it fails to interact with RhopH3.
evidence: Inferred from altered localization pattern in knockdown

claim: RhopH3 traffics normally to rhoptries in GlcN-treated R2glmS parasites
source: By contrast, RhopH3 appeared to traffic normally in GlcN-treated R2glmS parasites, as indicated by its apical colocalization with RAP1 in merozoites.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging data in Figure 2D showing colocalization with RAP1

claim: CLAG3, RhopH2 and RhopH3 assemble into a complex either during or immediately after translation
source: Thus, CLAG3, RhopH2 and RhopH3 assemble into a complex either during or immediately after translation.
evidence: Inferred from co-depletion patterns in knockdown experiments

claim: RhopH3 reaches rhoptries in the absence of RhopH2
source: RhopH3 reaches rhoptries in the absence of RhopH2, but the other two components are either rendered unstable or mis-trafficked in each knockdown.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing RhopH3 colocalization with RAP1 in R2glmS knockdown

claim: CLAG3 and RhopH2 are either rendered unstable or mis-trafficked in the absence of RhopH3
source: RhopH3 reaches rhoptries in the absence of RhopH2, but the other two components are either rendered unstable or mis-trafficked in each knockdown.
evidence: Inferred from loss of CLAG3 and altered RhopH2 localization in R3glmS knockdown

claim: The unchanged intensity and distribution of RAP1 in both knockdowns excludes essential roles of RhopH2 or RhopH3 in trafficking unassociated proteins or in rhoptry formation
source: The unchanged intensity and distribution of RAP1 in both knockdowns excludes essential roles of RhopH2 or RhopH3 in trafficking unassociated proteins or in rhoptry formation.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing normal RAP1 localization in knockdowns

claim: GlcN had no measurable effect on egress and erythrocyte invasion by wild-type parasites
source: Dose-response studies revealed that GlcN had no measurable effect on egress and erythrocyte invasion by wild-type or R2glmS parasites (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by invasion assay data in Figure 2E

claim: GlcN had no measurable effect on egress and erythrocyte invasion by R2glmS parasites
source: Dose-response studies revealed that GlcN had no measurable effect on egress and erythrocyte invasion by wild-type or R2glmS parasites (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by invasion assay data in Figure 2E

claim: RhopH2 does not contribute to erythrocyte invasion
source: Because the R2glmS knockdown co-depletes both RhopH2 and CLAG3 (Figure 2C and D), fully preserved invasion in this parasite definitively refutes proposals that either of these proteins contributes to egress or invasion.
evidence: Inferred from preserved invasion in R2glmS knockdown that lacks RhopH2

claim: CLAG3 does not contribute to erythrocyte invasion
source: Because the R2glmS knockdown co-depletes both RhopH2 and CLAG3 (Figure 2C and D), fully preserved invasion in this parasite definitively refutes proposals that either of these proteins contributes to egress or invasion.
evidence: Inferred from preserved invasion in R2glmS knockdown that lacks CLAG3

claim: R3glmS exhibited a dose-dependent effect on invasion, with 4 mM GlcN decreasing the number of ring-infected cells by 52% ± 3.0%
source: By contrast, R3glmS exhibited a dose-dependent effect on invasion, with 4 mM GlcN decreasing the number of ring-infected cells by 52% ± 3.0% (p=0.002, n = 3).
evidence: Supported by quantitative invasion assay data in Figure 2E

claim: The invasion defect in R3glmS did not result from failed maturation or reduced merozoite number
source: This invasion defect did not result from failed maturation or reduced merozoite number because RAP1 labeling indicated that these were not compromised (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing normal RAP1 labeling

claim: Giemsa staining revealed extracellular merozoites in GlcN-treated R3glmS parasites
source: Giemsa staining revealed extracellular merozoites (red arrows, Figure 2F), excluding effects on host cell rupture or merozoite egress.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data in Figure 2F

claim: RhopH3 contributes to either host cell interaction or subsequent parasite internalization
source: These findings restrict RhopH3's precise contribution to a role in either host cell interaction or subsequent parasite internalization.
evidence: Inferred from invasion defect and presence of extracellular merozoites

claim: RhopH3 is the sole RhopH complex member participating in invasion
source: Notably, the observed CLAG3 co-depletion mandated examination of both knockdowns and the serendipitously intact RhopH3 trafficking in R2glmS to exclude contributions from RhopH2 and CLAG3, and to determine that RhopH3 is the sole member participating in invasion.
evidence: Inferred from comparing invasion phenotypes in R2glmS and R3glmS knockdowns

claim: GlcN-treated R2glmS and R3glmS parasites progress normally to the trophozoite stage after invasion
source: We continued cultivation of GlcN-induced knockdowns and observed that these parasites progressed normally to the next trophozoite stage (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by observation of parasite development

claim: GlcN treatment results in complete loss of all three RhopH complex members in trophozoite-stage R2glmS and R3glmS parasites
source: Harvest and immunoblotting at this stage revealed complete loss, not only of the targeted proteins, but also of each other RhopH complex member (Figure 3B), a finding we confirmed with immunofluorescence assays (IFAs, Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 3B and immunofluorescence data in Figure 3C

claim: RhopH3 failed to transfer to new erythrocytes in GlcN-treated R2glmS despite retaining its rhoptry trafficking and invasion-associated functions
source: Interestingly, even RhopH3, which retained its rhoptry trafficking and invasion-associated functions in the RhopH2 knockdown (Figure 2D and E), failed to transfer to new erythrocytes in GlcN-treated R2glmS.
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting and immunofluorescence data showing absence of RhopH3 in trophozoites

claim: RhopH proteins require interactions with their cognate partners for successful transfer to the next erythrocyte at the time of invasion
source: As GlcN was without effect in untransfected parasites (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), these findings indicate that these proteins require interactions with their cognate partners for successful transfer to the next erythrocyte at the time of invasion.
evidence: Inferred from failure of transfer in knockdowns and specificity of GlcN effect

claim: The data argue against transfer of rhoptry proteins by simple entrapment in the nascent parasitophorous vacuole during invasion
source: They argue against transfer by simple entrapment of rhoptry proteins in the nascent parasitophorous vacuole during invasion (Kats et al., 2008).
evidence: Inferred from requirement for intact complex for transfer

claim: The unaffected morphology of trophozoite-stage parasites despite undetectable RhopH protein levels suggests normal formation of the parasitophorous vacuole and its surrounding membrane
source: The unaffected morphology of trophozoite-stage parasites, despite undetectable RhopH protein levels (Figure 3B and C), suggests normal formation of the parasitophorous vacuole (PV) and its surrounding membrane (PVM).
evidence: Inferred from normal parasite morphology in knockdowns

claim: Export of KAHRP and SBP1 into the host cytosol is unchanged in RhopH knockdowns
source: Export of two parasite proteins, KAHRP and SBP1, into the host cytosol was also unchanged (Figure 3C), suggesting that neither RhopH member contributes to the protein export translocon at this membrane (de Koning-Ward et al., 2009; Beck et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3C and cited references

claim: Neither RhopH2 nor RhopH3 contributes to the protein export translocon at the PVM
source: Export of two parasite proteins, KAHRP and SBP1, into the host cytosol was also unchanged (Figure 3C), suggesting that neither RhopH member contributes to the protein export translocon at this membrane (de Koning-Ward et al., 2009; Beck et al., 2014).
evidence: Inferred from unchanged export of other proteins in knockdowns

claim: Loss of the RhopH complex does not adversely affect a large conductance channel on the PVM
source: Cell-attached patch-clamp of the PVM in the R3glmS knockdown revealed that loss of the RhopH complex does not adversely affect a large conductance channel on this membrane (Desai et al., 1993; Desai and Rosenberg, 1997).
evidence: Supported by patch-clamp recordings in Figure 3D and cited references

claim: The R3glmS knockdown exhibited single-channel conductance, sub-conductance states, and channel voltage dependence matching those reported previously for the PVM channel
source: The R3glmS knockdown exhibited single-channel conductance, sub-conductance states, and channel voltage dependence matching those reported previously (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: Supported by patch-clamp data in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–D

claim: The PVM channel has a molecular composition distinct from that of PSAC
source: As knockdown abolishes PSAC activity at the host erythrocyte membrane (described below), these observations implicate a PVM channel molecular composition distinct from that of PSAC.
evidence: Inferred from preserved PVM channel activity despite loss of PSAC activity

claim: The findings exclude previously proposed roles for RhopH members in PV biogenesis
source: On the basis of the preserved structure and function at this membrane, our findings exclude previously proposed roles for RhopH members in PV biogenesis and suggest, instead, that these proteins only transit through this compartment.
evidence: Inferred from normal PV structure and function in knockdowns

claim: RhopH proteins only transit through the PV compartment
source: On the basis of the preserved structure and function at this membrane, our findings exclude previously proposed roles for RhopH members in PV biogenesis and suggest, instead, that these proteins only transit through this compartment.
evidence: Inferred from normal PV structure and function in knockdowns

claim: Sorbitol uptake was drastically reduced in both R2glmS and R3glmS after GlcN treatment
source: Using GlcN-treated parasites cultivated to the trophozoite stage, sorbitol uptake was drastically reduced in both R2glmS and R3glmS (p<0.001), but unaffected in the wild-type control (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: Supported by osmotic lysis kinetics data in Figure 4A–C

claim: GlcN treatment does not affect sorbitol uptake in wild-type parasites
source: Using GlcN-treated parasites cultivated to the trophozoite stage, sorbitol uptake was drastically reduced in both R2glmS and R3glmS (p<0.001), but unaffected in the wild-type control (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: Supported by osmotic lysis kinetics data in Figure 4A

claim: The EC50 values for GlcN in R2glmS and R3glmS are 0.26 ± 0.02 and 0.40 ± 0.02 mM, respectively
source: Interestingly, dose-response studies found EC50 values of 0.26 ± 0.02 and 0.40 ± 0.02 mM for GlcN, respectively (Figure 4D); these values are lower than those observed with GFP and DHFR reporter assays (Prommana et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by dose-response data in Figure 4D and comparison to cited reference

claim: There was a uniform reduction in the permeabilities of amino acid, sugar alcohol, and organic cation fluxes upon knockdown
source: There was also a uniform reduction in the permeabilities of amino acid, sugar alcohol, and organic cation fluxes upon knockdown (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by permeability measurements in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: Both knockdown parasites have a reduced number of channels with unaltered solute selectivities
source: These findings suggest that both knockdown parasites have a reduced number of channels with unaltered solute selectivities; this contrasts with previously characterized PSAC mutants, which exhibit unequal reductions in solute permeabilities as a consequence of altered single-channel properties (Hill et al., 2007; Lisk et al., 2008).
evidence: Inferred from uniform reduction in permeabilities across different solutes and comparison to cited references

claim: Wild-type and transfectant parasites without GlcN yielded indistinguishable Cl− conductances with characteristic inward-rectifying behavior
source: Without GlcN, wild-type and transfectant parasites yielded indistinguishable Cl–conductances with characteristic inward-rectifying behavior (apparent as larger downward deflections in an ensemble depiction of currents, Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp data in Figure 4F

claim: 4 mM GlcN produced a statistically insignificant reduction in Cl− conductance for wild-type cells
source: 4 mM GlcN produced a statistically insignificant reduction in Cl− conductance for wild-type cells (gCl, Figure 4G, n = 4–15 cells each).
evidence: Supported by quantitative conductance measurements in Figure 4G

claim: 4 mM GlcN abolished measurable PSAC-mediated currents on nearly all cells infected with R2glmS or R3glmS
source: By contrast, the same treatment abolished measurable PSAC-mediated currents on nearly all cells infected with R2glmS or R3glmS (n = 8–16 cells each), consistent with a large fraction of cells that are refractory to sorbitol uptake.
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp data in Figure 4F and 4G

claim: Recordings at increased gain identified residual channel activity on some GlcN-treated knockdown cells
source: Nevertheless, recordings at an increased gain managed to identify residual channel activity on some cells (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by high-gain patch-clamp recordings in Figure 4H

claim: The currents on GlcN-treated knockdown cells corresponded to a 250- to 400-fold reduction in functional PSAC copy number
source: The currents on these cells corresponded to a 250- to 400-fold reduction in functional PSAC copy number, but the preserved inward-rectifying behavior suggests that the few remaining channels have unmodified unitary properties.
evidence: Calculated from residual current measurements in Figure 4H

claim: The few remaining channels in GlcN-treated knockdown cells have unmodified unitary properties
source: The currents on these cells corresponded to a 250- to 400-fold reduction in functional PSAC copy number, but the preserved inward-rectifying behavior suggests that the few remaining channels have unmodified unitary properties.
evidence: Inferred from preserved inward-rectifying behavior in residual currents

claim: Opening and closing transitions from individual channels were detected in the whole-cell configuration in GlcN-treated knockdown cells
source: Remarkably, opening and closing transitions from individual channels were also detected despite the use of the whole-cell configuration (Figure 3H, traces beneath each ensemble).
evidence: Supported by single-channel transitions visible in whole-cell recordings in Figure 4H

claim: Cell-attached patch-clamp recordings obtained quantitatively similar results to whole-cell recordings
source: We also used the cell-attached patch-clamp configuration to record single channels on the surface of infected erythrocytes and obtained quantitatively similar results (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by cell-attached patch-clamp data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: RhopH protein knockdown reduces PSAC copy number without altering the properties of the remaining channel molecules
source: Thus, both organic solute uptake and patch-clamp studies indicate that RhopH protein knockdown reduces PSAC copy number without altering the properties of the remaining channel molecules.
evidence: Inferred from combined osmotic lysis and electrophysiology data

claim: GlcN exposure significantly inhibited growth of R2glmS and R3glmS in standard media
source: GlcN exposure significantly inhibited growth of R2glmS and R3glmS in standard media (Figure 4I, black bars; p<0.01 for comparisons to matched cultures without GlcN, n = 9 replicates from three independent trials each).
evidence: Supported by growth assay data in Figure 4I

claim: Each transfectant's growth was compromised to a greater extent in the reduced-nutrient PGIM compared to standard medium
source: Each transfectant's growth was compromised to a greater extent in the reduced-nutrient PGIM (red bars, p=0.02 when compared to growth reduction in standard medium).
evidence: Supported by growth assay data in Figure 4I comparing standard medium and PGIM

claim: GlcN exposure did not affect wild-type parasites in either standard medium or PGIM
source: GlcN exposure did not affect wild-type parasites in either medium, excluding nonspecific toxicity.
evidence: Supported by growth assay data in Figure 4I

claim: Greater growth inhibition in the nutrient-restricted PGIM provides molecular validation of a role for PSAC in nutrient uptake at the host membrane
source: Greater growth inhibition in the nutrient-restricted PGIM parallels the enhanced potency of PSAC inhibitors in this medium and provides molecular validation of a role for PSAC in nutrient uptake at the host membrane.
evidence: Inferred from differential growth inhibition in different media and comparison to PSAC inhibitor studies

claim: Integrations of DDD as an N-terminal tag after the predicted signal peptide cleavage sites were unsuccessful for both rhoph2 and rhoph3 genes
source: Repeated attempts to add DDD as an N-terminal tag after the predicted signal peptide cleavage sites were unsuccessful for both genes (Supplementary file 1), but integrations were readily obtained with C-terminal tagging (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by transfection attempts and integration data

claim: Integrations of DDD as a C-terminal tag were readily obtained for both rhoph2 and rhoph3 genes
source: Repeated attempts to add DDD as an N-terminal tag after the predicted signal peptide cleavage sites were unsuccessful for both genes (Supplementary file 1), but integrations were readily obtained with C-terminal tagging (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by successful transfection and integration data in Figure 5A

claim: Removal of TMP before the onset of gene transcription in R2-DDD yielded an 87% ± 9% decrease in channel activity
source: Removal of TMP before the onset of gene transcription in the preceding intracellular cycle yielded a maximal reduction in channel activity ('max', Figure 5B and C, 87% ± 9% and 35% ± 2% decrease for R2-DDD and R3-DDD, respectively; p<0.001 for both parasites, n = 3–4 trials each).
evidence: Supported by osmotic lysis kinetics data in Figure 5C

claim: Removal of TMP before the onset of gene transcription in R3-DDD yielded a 35% ± 2% decrease in channel activity
source: Removal of TMP before the onset of gene transcription in the preceding intracellular cycle yielded a maximal reduction in channel activity ('max', Figure 5B and C, 87% ± 9% and 35% ± 2% decrease for R2-DDD and R3-DDD, respectively; p<0.001 for both parasites, n = 3–4 trials each).
evidence: Supported by osmotic lysis kinetics data in Figure 5C

claim: TMP removal before merozoite egress led to reduced delivery of CLAG3 and RhopH3 upon invasion in R2-DDD
source: As also seen with the glmS knockdowns, TMP removal before merozoite egress led to reduced delivery of CLAG3 and RhopH3 upon invasion (Figure 5F, LS), demonstrating that RhopH complex integrity is important for faithful transfer during invasion.
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 5F

claim: RhopH complex integrity is important for faithful transfer during invasion
source: As also seen with the glmS knockdowns, TMP removal before merozoite egress led to reduced delivery of CLAG3 and RhopH3 upon invasion (Figure 5F, LS), demonstrating that RhopH complex integrity is important for faithful transfer during invasion.
evidence: Inferred from reduced protein delivery when complex is disrupted before invasion

claim: TMP removal after invasion preserved CLAG3 and RhopH3 levels in R2-DDD
source: Importantly, TMP removal after invasion preserved CLAG3 and RhopH3 levels (Figure 5F, ER).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 5F

claim: TMP removal after invasion in R2-DDD exhibited significantly reduced permeability
source: Nevertheless, these cells exhibited significantly reduced permeability (p=0.02, n=3), indicating that RhopH2 serves a role in channel formation beyond simply delivering the other RhopH components to invaded erythrocytes.
evidence: Supported by osmotic lysis data in Figure 5D and 5E

claim: RhopH2 serves a role in channel formation beyond simply delivering the other RhopH components to invaded erythrocytes
source: Nevertheless, these cells exhibited significantly reduced permeability (p=0.02, n=3), indicating that RhopH2 serves a role in channel formation beyond simply delivering the other RhopH components to invaded erythrocytes.
evidence: Inferred from reduced permeability despite preserved protein delivery

claim: 66% of CLAG3 in control cultures successfully inserted into the host membrane
source: While 66% of CLAG3 in control cultures successfully inserted into the host membrane, TMP removal in early rings yielded reduced protease susceptibility (Figure 5H, p<0.01 from quantification of band intensities); TMP removal from late schizonts (LS) produced a similar reduction in CLAG3 insertion at the host membrane, compounding the reduced delivery during invasion described above.
evidence: Supported by protease susceptibility data quantified in Figure 5H

claim: TMP removal in early rings yielded reduced CLAG3 protease susceptibility in R2-DDD
source: While 66% of CLAG3 in control cultures successfully inserted into the host membrane, TMP removal in early rings yielded reduced protease susceptibility (Figure 5H, p<0.01 from quantification of band intensities); TMP removal from late schizonts (LS) produced a similar reduction in CLAG3 insertion at the host membrane, compounding the reduced delivery during invasion described above.
evidence: Supported by protease susceptibility data in Figure 5G and quantification in Figure 5H

claim: RhopH2 destabilization after invasion interferes with both CLAG3 membrane insertion and induction of PSAC activity
source: Thus, RhopH2 destabilization after invasion interferes with both CLAG3 membrane insertion and induction of PSAC activity.
evidence: Inferred from reduced protease susceptibility and reduced permeability in ER knockdown

claim: Cultivation without TMP adversely affected the expansion of R2-DDD cultures within a single developmental cycle
source: Cultivation without TMP adversely affected the expansion of cultures within a single developmental cycle (red triangles, Figure 5I), indicating that any residual channel activity is insufficient to meet parasite nutrient demand.
evidence: Supported by growth data in Figure 5I

claim: Any residual channel activity in R2-DDD knockdown is insufficient to meet parasite nutrient demand
source: Cultivation without TMP adversely affected the expansion of cultures within a single developmental cycle (red triangles, Figure 5I), indicating that any residual channel activity is insufficient to meet parasite nutrient demand.
evidence: Inferred from growth inhibition in knockdown

claim: Continued cultivation without TMP for two months did not produce outgrowth of resistant parasites
source: Continued cultivation without TMP for two months did not produce outgrowth of resistant parasites, revealing that changes in other host- or parasite-derived nutrient uptake mechanisms cannot compensate for the loss of the RhopH-associated channel.
evidence: Supported by long-term cultivation data in Figure 5I

claim: Changes in other host- or parasite-derived nutrient uptake mechanisms cannot compensate for the loss of the RhopH-associated channel
source: Continued cultivation without TMP for two months did not produce outgrowth of resistant parasites, revealing that changes in other host- or parasite-derived nutrient uptake mechanisms cannot compensate for the loss of the RhopH-associated channel.
evidence: Inferred from failure to generate resistant parasites over extended cultivation

claim: Restoration of TMP after two, four, or six days permitted parasite recovery with increasing lag periods
source: Restoration of TMP after two, four, or six days permitted parasite recovery with increasing lag periods (circles), consistent with an increasing fraction of irreversibly affected parasites.
evidence: Supported by recovery data in Figure 5I

claim: RhopH3 undergoes proteolytic processing near its C-terminus
source: We found that the relatively weak PSAC inhibition in R3-DDD upon TMP removal results from proteolytic processing of RhopH3 near its C-terminus (Figure 6A, arrow).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 6B and 6C showing cleavage products

claim: Immunoblotting with an antibody against the 3xHA epitope tag revealed both the unprocessed 130 kDa RhopH3 protein and a ~30 kDa soluble cleavage product
source: Immunoblotting with an antibody against the 3xHA epitope tag added through transfection revealed both the unprocessed 130 kDa protein and a ~30 kDa soluble cleavage product (Figure 6B, red arrow).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 6B

claim: A RhopH3-specific antibody detected two bands of 100 and 130 kDa, differing in size as predicted by the release of a single downstream fragment
source: A RhopH3-specific antibody confirmed this processing as it detected two bands of 100 and 130 kDa, differing in size as predicted by the release of a single downstream fragment (Figure 6A and C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 6C

claim: The downstream fragment's size implicates processing at 8–10 kDa upstream of the native C-terminus
source: The downstream fragment's size implicates processing at 8–10 kDa upstream of the native C-terminus (Figure 6A, arrow).
evidence: Calculated from fragment sizes observed in immunoblots

claim: RhopH3 processing occurs soon after protein synthesis
source: The fragment's presence only in schizonts and a relatively weak signal for the residual uncleaved form after invasion indicates near-complete processing soon after protein synthesis (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: Inferred from stage-specific detection of cleavage products in Figure 6B–D

claim: A strong anti-HA signal associated with rhoptries suggests RhopH3 processing occurs at this site
source: A strong anti-HA signal associated with rhoptries suggests processing at this site (Figure 6D), consistent with known protease activity in this organelle (Sam-Yellowe et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 6D and cited reference on rhoptry protease activity

claim: The cleaved C-terminal fragment of RhopH3 appears to be rapidly degraded
source: The cleaved C-terminal fragment appears to be rapidly degraded, as it was absent from both spent culture medium and invaded cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: Inferred from absence of fragment in culture medium and invaded cells in Figure 6B

claim: TMP removal rendered all three RhopH proteins undetectable in the R2-DDD parasite
source: While TMP removal rendered all three RhopH proteins undetectable in the R2-DDD parasite, these proteins and their transfer to trophozoites were preserved in R3-DDD (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 6E

claim: RhopH proteins and their transfer to trophozoites were preserved in R3-DDD after TMP removal
source: While TMP removal rendered all three RhopH proteins undetectable in the R2-DDD parasite, these proteins and their transfer to trophozoites were preserved in R3-DDD (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 6E

claim: The processed 100 kDa RhopH3 protein was minimally affected by cultivation without TMP for 48 hr
source: Immunoblotting revealed that the processed 100 kDa RhopH3 protein was minimally affected by cultivation without TMP for 48 hr; other members of the complex were also unaffected (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 6F

claim: The unprocessed 130 kDa RhopH3 isoform is TMP-sensitive
source: Probing with anti-HA revealed that the unprocessed 130 kDa RhopH3 isoform is TMP-sensitive, consistent with the idea that any RhopH3 that escapes proteolytic processing can be conditionally degraded through the DDD tag.
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 6F showing loss of 130 kDa band

claim: Uncleaved RhopH3 is successfully transferred to the next erythrocyte upon invasion
source: The biological significance of processing is unclear as uncleaved RhopH3 is still successfully transferred to the next erythrocyte upon invasion (Figure 6B and D, anti-HA signal).
evidence: Supported by detection of anti-HA signal in invaded cells in Figure 6B and 6D

claim: Imaging did not detect export of the unprocessed RhopH3 form from the PV
source: As imaging did not detect export of the unprocessed form from the PV (Figure 6C, anti-HA signal in trophozoites), one possibility is that processing facilitates RhopH3 export to the host cytoplasm.
evidence: Supported by absence of anti-HA signal in trophozoite host cytoplasm in Figure 6D

claim: Processing may facilitate RhopH3 export to the host cytoplasm
source: As imaging did not detect export of the unprocessed form from the PV (Figure 6C, anti-HA signal in trophozoites), one possibility is that processing facilitates RhopH3 export to the host cytoplasm.
evidence: Speculated based on differential localization of processed and unprocessed forms

claim: PTEX knockdown abolishes the development of PSAC-mediated uptake
source: Using the 13F10 HSP101-DDD clone (Beck et al., 2014), we confirmed that PTEX knockdown abolishes the development of PSAC-mediated uptake (Figure 7A) and we then examined RhopH protein export (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by osmotic lysis data in Figure 7A and cited reference

claim: Export of RhopH2 was fully blocked in trophozoite-stage parasites grown for 48 hr without TMP in the HSP101-DDD clone
source: Remarkably, export of RhopH2 and of RhopH3 were both fully blocked in trophozoite-stage parasites grown for 48 hr without TMP.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 7B showing colocalization with HRP2 in PV

claim: Export of RhopH3 was fully blocked in trophozoite-stage parasites grown for 48 hr without TMP in the HSP101-DDD clone
source: Remarkably, export of RhopH2 and of RhopH3 were both fully blocked in trophozoite-stage parasites grown for 48 hr without TMP.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 7B showing colocalization with HRP2 in PV

claim: RhopH2 and RhopH3 were trapped in the vacuole upon PTEX knockdown
source: Colocalization with HRP2, a parasite protein carrying the canonical PEXEL export signal (Beck et al., 2014), showed that both proteins were trapped in the vacuole upon PTEX knockdown.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence colocalization data in Figure 7B and cited reference

claim: CLAG3 export requires PTEX activity
source: In contrast to the earlier study, we also found that CLAG3 export requires PTEX activity as TMP removal prevented its movement out of the PV (Figure 7B bottom row; colocalization with SBP1, another PTEX substrate; Beck et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 7B and cited reference

claim: CLAG3 fails to reach the host membrane upon PTEX block
source: This revealed complete loss of CLAG3 protease susceptibility upon TMP removal (Figure 7C), sidestepping concerns about imaging conditions and indicating that CLAG3 fails to reach the host membrane upon PTEX block.
evidence: Supported by protease susceptibility data in Figure 7C

claim: RhopH proteins are delivered to the PV upon invasion and then require PTEX for export at the PVM
source: Thus, RhopH proteins are delivered to the PV upon invasion and then require PTEX for export at the PVM.
evidence: Inferred from blocked export in PTEX knockdown

claim: Both R2-DDD and 13F10 knockdown parasites completed their intracellular cycle and invaded new erythrocytes normally
source: Both knockdown parasites completed their intracellular cycle and invaded new erythrocytes normally, consistent with already fulfilled requirements for protein export and nutrient uptake and with the relatively slow kinetics of DDD destabilization.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data in Figure 7D

claim: After invasion, development was arrested in both R2-DDD and 13F10 parasites after TMP removal
source: After invasion, development was arrested in both parasites, with neither being capable of completing schizogony (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data in Figure 7D and 7E

claim: 13F10 parasites appeared to arrest at an earlier stage than R2-DDD parasites
source: Interestingly, 13F10 parasites appeared to arrest at an earlier stage than R2-DDD parasites (48 hr timepoint, Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by comparative microscopy data in Figure 7D

claim: The earlier demise of 13F10 parasites may reflect either contributions from the loss of other exported activities or a lower residual PSAC activity in 13F10 than in R2-DDD parasites
source: This earlier demise may reflect either contributions from the loss of other exported activities or a lower residual PSAC activity in 13F10 than in R2-DDD parasites.
evidence: Speculated based on differential arrest timing

claim: The RhopH complex was identified in early proteomic studies of invasive merozoites
source: One multi-protein complex, the RhopH complex, was identified in early proteomic studies of invasive merozoites (Campbell et al., 1984; Holder et al., 1985), but remains poorly characterized.
evidence: Supported by cited references

claim: The RhopH complex is a high-molecular weight complex localizing to rhoptries
source: Its name recognizes that it is a high-molecular weight complex localizing to rhoptries, which are specialized organelles at the apical end of the merozoite (Holder et al., 1985; Cooper et al., 1988; Kaneko et al., 2001; Ling et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by cited references

claim: Each of the three RhopH complex member proteins are synthesized in mature intracellular parasites known as schizonts
source: Each of the three member proteins, termed CLAG (or RhopH1), RhopH2, and RhopH3, are synthesized in mature intracellular parasites known as schizonts (Kaneko et al., 2001, 2005).
evidence: Supported by cited references

claim: Upon egress, RhopH proteins are secreted, along with other rhoptry contents, onto the erythrocyte targeted for invasion
source: Upon egress, these proteins are secreted, along with other rhoptry contents, onto the erythrocyte targeted for invasion.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of rhoptry protein secretion

claim: It has been assumed that the RhopH complex serves a role in invasion
source: It has therefore been assumed that the RhopH complex serves a role in invasion; because a fraction of this complex is transferred to the new host cell, another proposal has been that these proteins contribute to formation of the parasitophorous vacuole that surrounds the internalized parasite (Kaneko, 2007; Ocampo et al., 2005; Ranjan et al., 2011; Cortés et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by cited references proposing these roles

claim: Genetic mapping in P. falciparum implicated the CLAG paralogs on chromosome 3, CLAG3.1 and CLAG3.2, in the formation of PSAC
source: Surprisingly, genetic mapping in P. falciparum subsequently implicated the CLAG paralogs on chromosome 3, CLAG3.1 and CLAG3.2, in the formation of the plasmodial surface anion channel (PSAC; Nguitragool et al., 2011), a nutrient and ion channel at the host cell membrane (Desai et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by cited references

claim: PSAC is a nutrient and ion channel at the host cell membrane
source: Surprisingly, genetic mapping in P. falciparum subsequently implicated the CLAG paralogs on chromosome 3, CLAG3.1 and CLAG3.2, in the formation of the plasmodial surface anion channel (PSAC; Nguitragool et al., 2011), a nutrient and ion channel at the host cell membrane (Desai et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by cited references

claim: Subsequent studies with transport mutants and specific inhibitors have strengthened the evidence for CLAG3 and possibly CLAG2 in channel activity
source: Subsequent studies with transport mutants and specific inhibitors have strengthened the evidence for CLAG3 and possibly CLAG2 in channel activity (Pillai et al., 2012; Sharma et al., 2013; Mira-Martinez et al., 2013; Sharma et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by cited references

claim: Conservation of both the RhopH complex and PSAC activity in all examined Plasmodia spp. suggests a causal link
source: Although conservation of both the RhopH complex and PSAC activity in all examined Plasmodia spp. suggests a causal link (Lisk and Desai, 2005), the precise contribution of these proteins to either the activation of channels or the formation of the nutrient pore is unclear (Desai, 2012).
evidence: Supported by cited references and inference from conservation

claim: Growth defects in a reported CLAG3 knockout are consistent with a role in nutrient uptake, but could also result from the loss of other activities
source: Growth defects in a reported CLAG3 knockout are consistent with a role in nutrient uptake, but could also result from the loss of other activities (Comeaux et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by cited reference and inference about alternative explanations

claim: rhoph2 and rhoph3 are present as single copy genes in each Plasmodium species
source: In contrast to the clag gene family, rhoph2 and rhoph3 are present as single copy genes in each Plasmodium species.
evidence: Based on genomic knowledge of Plasmodium species

claim: Both RhopH2 and RhopH3 proteins are essential for parasite survival
source: Our studies show that both proteins are essential for parasite survival.
evidence: Supported by inability to generate knockouts and growth defects in knockdowns

claim: RhopH3, but not RhopH2 or CLAG3, contributes to erythrocyte invasion
source: RhopH3, but not RhopH2 or CLAG3, contributes to erythrocyte invasion.
evidence: Supported by invasion assay data comparing knockdowns

claim: The formation and functional properties of the parasitophorous vacuole are preserved in RhopH knockdowns
source: Because the formation and functional properties of the parasitophorous vacuole are preserved in our knockdowns, these three proteins do not appear to serve long-assumed roles in vacuole biogenesis.
evidence: Supported by normal PV morphology and PVM channel activity in knockdowns

claim: RhopH2, RhopH3, and CLAG3 do not appear to serve long-assumed roles in vacuole biogenesis
source: Because the formation and functional properties of the parasitophorous vacuole are preserved in our knockdowns, these three proteins do not appear to serve long-assumed roles in vacuole biogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from preserved PV structure and function in knockdowns

claim: Both RhopH2 and RhopH3 are required for successful PSAC formation
source: Instead, organic solute uptake and electrophysiological studies reveal that both RhopH2 and RhopH3 are required for successful PSAC formation; loss of channel activity leads to rapid parasite demise.
evidence: Supported by osmotic lysis and patch-clamp data in knockdowns

claim: Loss of channel activity leads to rapid parasite demise
source: Instead, organic solute uptake and electrophysiological studies reveal that both RhopH2 and RhopH3 are required for successful PSAC formation; loss of channel activity leads to rapid parasite demise.
evidence: Supported by growth inhibition and arrest data in knockdowns

claim: The RhopH complex is an attractive therapeutic target
source: These critical functions and the elaborate stage-specific trafficking we report makes the RhopH complex an attractive therapeutic target.
evidence: Inferred from essentiality and dual functions of the complex

claim: Malaria parasites are sophisticated single-celled organisms that infect erythrocytes of many vertebrate animals
source: Malaria parasites are sophisticated single-celled organisms that infect erythrocytes of many vertebrate animals; in humans, the virulent Plasmodium falciparum pathogen remains a public health priority because of high mortality rates and global economic costs.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about malaria parasites

claim: In humans, the virulent Plasmodium falciparum pathogen remains a public health priority because of high mortality rates and global economic costs
source: Malaria parasites are sophisticated single-celled organisms that infect erythrocytes of many vertebrate animals; in humans, the virulent Plasmodium falciparum pathogen remains a public health priority because of high mortality rates and global economic costs.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about malaria public health impact

claim: Malaria parasites have evolved novel proteins, some of which form multi-subunit complexes, to mediate host cell invasion and to enable intracellular survival
source: These parasites have evolved novel proteins, some of which form multi-subunit complexes, to mediate host cell invasion and to enable intracellular survival.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about parasite biology

claim: Cotranslational assembly of the three-member RhopH complex enables trafficking to the rhoptry
source: Cotranslational assembly of the three-member RhopH complex enables trafficking to the rhophtry ('1').
evidence: Inferred from co-depletion patterns and trafficking defects in knockdowns, illustrated in Figure 8

claim: After merozoite egress, only RhopH3 contributes to invasion
source: After merozoite egress, only RhopH3 contributes to invasion ('2'); the complex is then deposited into the PV ('3'), from where it is exported via PTEX ('4') and trafficked via the Maurer's clefts (MC, '5') to the host RBC membrane.
evidence: Supported by invasion assay data and illustrated in Figure 8

claim: The RhopH complex is deposited into the PV after invasion
source: After merozoite egress, only RhopH3 contributes to invasion ('2'); the complex is then deposited into the PV ('3'), from where it is exported via PTEX ('4') and trafficked via the Maurer's clefts (MC, '5') to the host RBC membrane.
evidence: Supported by localization and PTEX knockdown data, illustrated in Figure 8

claim: The RhopH complex is exported from the PV via PTEX
source: After merozoite egress, only RhopH3 contributes to invasion ('2'); the complex is then deposited into the PV ('3'), from where it is exported via PTEX ('4') and trafficked via the Maurer's clefts (MC, '5') to the host RBC membrane.
evidence: Supported by PTEX knockdown data showing blocked export, illustrated in Figure 8

claim: The RhopH complex is trafficked via the Maurer's clefts to the host RBC membrane
source: After merozoite egress, only RhopH3 contributes to invasion ('2'); the complex is then deposited into the PV ('3'), from where it is exported via PTEX ('4') and trafficked via the Maurer's clefts (MC, '5') to the host RBC membrane.
evidence: Inferred from known role of Maurer's clefts in protein export, illustrated in Figure 8

claim: At the host RBC membrane, the RhopH complex determines nutrient uptake via PSAC
source: There, the complex determines nutrient uptake via PSAC ('6').
evidence: Supported by loss of PSAC activity in knockdowns, illustrated in Figure 8

claim: Early studies predicted that parasite proteins involved in PSAC would be translated in ring- or trophozoite-stage parasites, just prior to the onset of solute uptake
source: Early studies predicted that parasite proteins that are involved in the PSAC would be translated in ring- or trophozoite-stage parasites, just prior to the onset of solute uptake (Kutner et al., 1982).
evidence: Supported by cited reference

claim: Genetic mapping identified CLAG3 as a PSAC determinant and contradicted predictions about timing of protein synthesis
source: Genetic mapping identified CLAG3 as a PSAC determinant and contradicted these predictions (Nguitragool et al., 2011); production of CLAG3 in the prior cycle and packaging into rhoptries seemed to be inconsistent with a primary role for CLAG3 in channel formation.
evidence: Supported by cited reference and inference about inconsistency

claim: The unexpectedly early synthesis and complicated trafficking of RhopH proteins evolved to enable two distinct functions at separate points in the parasite cycle
source: Molecular evidence for a RhopH3 role in erythrocyte invasion, as we now provide, suggests that this unexpectedly early synthesis and complicated trafficking evolved to enable two distinct functions at separate points in the parasite cycle.
evidence: Inferred from dual functions identified in this study

claim: All three members of the RhopH complex are conserved in plasmodia but have no clear orthologs in other apicomplexan parasites
source: Whether the role in invasion or in nutrient uptake arose first and how the second function was added is unclear as all three members of the RhopH complex are conserved in plasmodia but have no clear orthologs in other apicomplexan parasites.
evidence: Based on comparative genomics knowledge

claim: The RhopH complex presumably acquired both functions early in adaption to erythrocytes as both are essential for survival in the vertebrate bloodstream
source: The RhopH complex presumably acquired both functions early in adaption to erythrocytes as both are essential for survival in the vertebrate bloodstream.
evidence: Speculated based on essentiality of both functions

claim: P. falciparum utilizes multiple receptor-ligand interactions for invasion
source: How might loss of this protein interfere with successful erythrocyte invasion? As P. falciparum utilizes multiple receptor-ligand interactions for invasion, one possibility is that RhopH3 interacts directly with an erythrocyte receptor.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about P. falciparum invasion mechanisms

claim: A yeast-two hybrid screen and binding studies with a recombinant C-terminal fragment of RhopH3 suggest that the anion exchanger Band3 protein might be the receptor
source: A yeast-two hybrid screen and binding studies with a recombinant C-terminal fragment of RhopH3 suggest that the anion exchanger Band3 protein might be the receptor (Baldwin et al., 2014), a proposal supported by the inhibitory effects of specific RhopH3 antibodies (Ranjan et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by cited references

claim: Quantitative loss of host cell permeability in RhopH2 and RhopH3 knockdowns provides evidence against the induced upregulation of human channels by the parasite
source: Quantitative loss of host cell permeability in RhopH2 and RhopH3 knockdowns addresses two important uncertainties about nutrient and ion uptake by infected cells. Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings on the conditional knockdowns reported here provide evidence against the induced upregulation of human channels by the parasite: near-complete removal of RhopH-associated channels showed stochastic transitions from the handful of remaining functional PSACs but failed to uncover unrelated currents (Figure 4H; Staines et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by patch-clamp data in Figure 4H and cited reference

claim: CLAG3's paucity of predicted transmembrane domains and lack of homology to known channel proteins raised doubts about whether this protein could form a pore in isolation
source: Although several studies have supported a CLAG3 role in PSAC formation (Nguitragool et al., 2011; Pillai et al., 2012; Sharma et al., 2013; Mira-Martinez et al., 2013), its paucity of predicted transmembrane domains and lack of homology to known channel proteins raised doubts about whether this protein could form a pore in isolation.
evidence: Based on structural analysis and comparison to known channels, with cited references

claim: Stable association of CLAG3 with two other membrane proteins and their requirement for channel activity makes the direct formation of the channel pore by the RhopH complex more plausible
source: Stable association with two other membrane proteins and their requirement for channel activity makes the direct formation of the channel pore by the RhopH complex more plausible.
evidence: Inferred from co-depletion and functional data

claim: Genetic mapping of transport inhibition by proteases to the clag3 locus supports the model that the RhopH complex directly forms the channel pore
source: This model is also supported by genetic mapping of transport inhibition by proteases to the clag3 locus (Nguitragool et al., 2014), by an amphipathic transmembrane domain that appears to line a water-filled pore (Sharma et al., 2015), and by site-directed mutagenesis of critical residues that define PSAC behavior (Sharma et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by cited references

claim: PSAC activity is an established drug target, validated with derivatives of a potent inhibitor and with molecular approaches
source: PSAC activity is already an established drug target, validated with derivatives of a potent inhibitor and with molecular approaches (Pillai et al., 2010, 2012); present studies).
evidence: Supported by cited references and current study

claim: PSAC is the main exported activity cited as the basis of in vitro growth inhibition upon PTEX knockdown
source: This channel is also the main exported activity cited as the basis of in vitro growth inhibition upon PTEX knockdown (Beck et al., 2014; Elsworth et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by cited references

claim: Inhibitors that interact with one or more members of the RhopH complex may disrupt disease progression by inhibiting both parasite invasion and nutrient acquisition
source: Inhibitors that interact with one or more members of this essential complex may disrupt disease progression by inhibiting both parasite invasion and nutrient acquisition.
evidence: Speculated based on dual functions of the complex
